description: Why your shoelaces come undone, at MSN-chat pace: granny versus square, the Ian knot, and a live demo where one crossing locks and the other slips.
buddyStat: granny vs square, and the Ian knot
composeNote: This is a recorded conversation. Toggle and pull in the demo above.
disclosure: Starter draft. The granny-versus-square structure is standard knot lore; the demo draws only a schematic of the two crossings. Background paraphrased from Ian's Shoelace Site and Wikipedia.

editorial.reader: A curious reader who knows the surface term but wants the mechanism.
editorial.problem: The reader recognizes the vocabulary of shoelace knots but can't yet predict what the mechanism will do.
editorial.thesis: The page should leave the reader able to explain shoelace knots in plain language and predict their behavior.
evidence: The conversation cites its sources and the demos make the mechanism visible.
The understanding check names common misconceptions and explains every answer.
editorial.uncertainty: The demos teach the model and stop short of a measurement or a full treatment.

understanding.intro: Before you run off to re-tie those shoes, a quick check. Five questions, no stakes. If the demo did its job, you already know every answer.

questions.q: Before you toggle the demo to granny, predict: which rope will sit on top at each of the two crossings?

options.t: red on top at both crossings, the same rope over twice
options.why: The demo keeps crossing one fixed with red over and flips only crossing two. Granny repeats the first move, so red goes over again. Toggle back and blue takes the second crossing: that change alone is the whole square-versus-granny difference.

options.t: red on top at the first, then blue on top at the second
options.why: That's the square you start on. The verdict under the canvas says it: the square's second crossing mirrors the first, so the other rope goes over. Granny is the setting where nothing alternates.

options.t: blue on top at both, since granny flips the first crossing
options.why: The toggle never touches crossing one. Red stays over there in both modes; the only thing the toggle changes is who goes over at the second crossing.

options.t: blue on top at the first and red on top at the second
options.why: That's a square seen in a mirror: the crossings still oppose, so it would hold. A granny needs the second crossing to repeat the first, the same rope over twice.

questions.q: A sailor says the reef knot holds because sailors cinch it harder than kids tie shoes. What's the flaw?

options.t: the demo pulls both knots equally hard, and only the granny slides
options.why: Same pull, opposite outcomes, so tension can't be what decides. The square holds because each rope nips the other flat; the granny is unbalanced and capsizes however hard you pull it.

options.t: none, since tension is what makes any knot hold in the end
options.why: Run the demo both ways: one pull button, one pull strength, and only one knot locks. Whatever decides it has to be something the two knots differ on, and the toggle changes just one crossing.

options.t: the reef knot has a third crossing, and that one does the locking
options.why: Both knots are exactly two crossings. The toggle in the demo never adds one; it only flips which rope goes over at the second.

options.t: sail rope is stiffer than laces, so its friction does the holding
options.why: The chat runs one argument from a reef knot on a sail to the bow on your shoe. Same two crossings, same verdict, whatever the rope is made of.

questions.q: People credit the Ian knot with keeping their laces tied. What does it actually change?

options.t: only the speed: it gets you to the same square bow faster
options.why: That is the trick. Both loops form at once and pass through each other in one motion, so you land on the same square bow in a fraction of the time. Speed method, same destination.

options.t: it's a third kind of knot that holds better than square or granny
options.why: Ian Fieggen's method produces the ordinary square bow. The speed comes from forming both loops simultaneously, and the holding comes from the same opposed crossings as any square knot.

options.t: it adds a tuck that pins the bow so it can't work loose
options.why: The tuck belongs to his Secure variant, an add-on for laces that still wander. The base Ian knot is pure speed: two simultaneous loops, one motion, same square bow at the end.

options.t: it makes handedness irrelevant, you get a square bow either way
options.why: Handedness still rules. Tied with the right handedness it gives the square bow, which means the wrong handedness gives you a very fast granny. The crossings still decide whether it holds.

questions.q: Your bow sits diagonally and works loose. To fix it you flip both your starting cross and your wrap. What do you get?

options.t: a granny again, mirrored, since the two steps still match
options.why: Granny is a relation between the two steps. Flip both and they still go the same way, so you've tied the granny's mirror image. Reverse just one, as the chat says, and the bow sits straight across.

options.t: a square bow, because the whole knot now has the other handedness
options.why: Handedness of the whole knot is beside the point; what counts is whether step two opposes step one. Flipping both keeps them matched, and a matched pair is the granny.

options.t: a square bow that sits straight, as long as you cinch it hard
options.why: Two fixes stacked, and neither works. Both steps still match, so it's a granny, and the demo already showed that pulling harder makes a granny slide apart.

options.t: a third kind of knot, neither the square nor the granny
options.why: Two crossings can only match or oppose, so there are just the two outcomes. Flipping both keeps them matched: the granny you started with, seen in a mirror.

questions.q: Last one. Three friends tie bows: standard, bunny ears, and Ian. Two hold, one slips. What do you check on the slipping one?

options.t: whether its two crossings match, which shows as a diagonal sit
options.why: Every method lands on the same two crossings, and only their handedness decides. A granny bow sits diagonally across the shoe, so you can spot it before it falls open. Push back: if the slipper was the Ian knot, the answer stays the same.

options.t: which method it used, since bunny ears is the weakest of the three
options.why: The chat says bunny ears is just as prone to the granny trap as the others, and no more. Any of the three can land on a square or a granny; the method only sets the speed and the route.

options.t: whether it skipped the Secure tuck that pins the loops in place
options.why: Partly right, the tuck exists for laces that wander. But a slipping bow is first a question about its crossings: the chat's fix for a bow that works loose is reversing one step, and the tuck is an add-on on top of a square.

options.t: how hard it was cinched, because a loose bow slips first
options.why: The demo already settled tension: one pull, and the square locks while the granny slides. Tighten a granny and it still capsizes.

messages.html: people swear by the "Ian knot" as the world's fastest shoelace knot, and that it stops their laces coming undone. is there real structure here or is it folklore?

Real structure, and it is the same argument as the oldest knot in the book: granny versus square. A knot like this is basically two crossings. If the second crossing mirrors the first you get a square (reef) knot that seats flat and holds. If the second repeats the first you get a granny that capsizes and slips. If your laces keep falling open, you're probably tying a granny bow without knowing it.

demo.bar: granny vs square · toggle the second crossing, then pull
demo.html:
Two ropes, two crossings. The only difference between a square knot and a granny is the handedness of the second crossing. Toggle it, then pull the ends.

Square (reef). The second crossing mirrors the first, so the knot seats flat and each rope nips the other. Pull and it locks.

messages.html: huh, the only difference is the handedness of the second crossing. so my laces slip because I cross the same way twice?

Exactly. The standard bow is cross, loop, wrap, pull. If your starting cross and your wrapping loop go the same way, you have built a granny bow: it sits diagonally across the shoe and works loose. Reverse just one of the two and you get a square bow that sits straight across and stays put. Same moves, opposite handedness on the second step.
ok so where does the Ian knot come in?

The Ian knot (Ian Fieggen's) is a speed method that lands on the same knot. You form a loop in each hand at the same time and pass them through each other in one motion, where the standard bow makes one loop and wraps the other lace around it. Tied with the right handedness it gives the same square bow, just much faster. His Secure variant adds a tuck for laces that still wander.
and bunny ears? that's what I learned as a kid.

Bunny ears makes both loops first, then ties the two like ropes. It is easy to learn and just as prone to the granny trap: tie the two ears with the same handedness you started with and you get a granny bow. Whatever method got you to the two crossings, only their handedness decides whether the knot holds.
so the whole thing reduces to: make the two crossings oppose.

That is the entire trick, from a reef knot on a sail to the bow on your shoe. Cross one way, then cross back the other. Match the handedness and it slips; oppose it and it holds. Everything else is speed and style.

I'm going to go re-tie my shoes. thanks.
